label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Jess, I know what you meant.

When you texted me last night that it was one assignment and I shouldn’t torch my job over it, I didn’t hear you saying the history didn’t matter. I heard a friend who knows what schools can do to teachers who become inconvenient. We met student teaching in 2012. You have enough information to be worried about me.

And when half the group chat agreed with you, I understood that, too. From outside my classroom, this probably looks straightforward: a parent objects to a project, the principal wants it gone, and I have plenty of other things I could teach. Pick another assignment. Get through November. Keep your head down.

I’d rather write this out than keep sending little defensive texts between dinner and grading. Not because I need everyone to agree with me. Mostly, Jess, I want you to understand why I’m keeping it.

The assignment is for my two sections of juniors in US History II. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston’s busing and school desegregation between 1974 and 1976. Ten minutes of recorded conversation, then a two-page reflection. I’ve done it for four years at Cobb Street High. Until now, nobody has complained.

That doesn’t automatically make it a good assignment. Four years without a complaint could mean four years of people being comfortable, or four years of people not telling me they weren’t.

This parent did tell someone. She emailed Dr. Halvorsen and copied a school committee member. She said the assignment “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.”

I don’t like having my assignment described that way. But I can see how it could feel that way to a kid looking at the instructions, imagining a conversation at the kitchen table, and wondering what happens if the answers are bad.

The family part is personal in ways I may have been too quick to call educational. I get to assign the interview and collect the reflection. The student has to keep living with whatever they learn, and with the person they learned it from. A teacher’s enthusiasm doesn’t make that pressure disappear.

So I’m changing that part.

My plan for the meeting on Thursday is to keep the project and add an alternative that doesn’t require interviewing family: a conversation with a librarian or archivist, or work with recorded interviews from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody should have to bring me a difficult family story to earn a grade. The alternative needs to be a real option, not something a kid has to ask for in front of everyone and then explain.

I think the parent has a point about pressure. I don’t think that means the project should disappear.

In 2023, a student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. Nobody in his family had heard her talk about it before.

He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class.

Afterward, nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute.

I’m wary of making that silence sound too perfect. I can’t tell you what every student was thinking, and I’m not going to pretend forty seconds of audio transformed a roomful of teenagers. But I remember sitting there, listening with them, and realizing how much was missing from the paragraph in our textbook.

Here was somebody’s grandmother, someone with a working life and a memory of those years, speaking in her own voice. D. had gone into the assignment knowing her as his grandmother. Now he knew something else about her.

That is a worthwhile thing for a history class to make possible.

Last year, another student learned that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

Even writing those two sentences next to each other makes me stop. Her being upset wasn’t a teaching achievement. A good paper doesn’t prove that the experience was worth it for her, and it certainly doesn’t give me permission to put every other student through something similar.

What stayed with me was how carefully she thought about what she had learned. She didn’t tidy it up. She didn’t pretend it was fine because he was family, and she didn’t suddenly know everything there was to know about him, either. She was trying to understand something difficult without making it easier than it was.

I want there to be room for that work in my classroom. I also want students to have some say in how close to home they do it.

One of my first reactions to the complaint was that the kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need this most. I still understand the impulse behind that thought, but I don’t entirely trust it. It’s awfully convenient for a teacher: if you’re interested, the assignment is working; if you’re distressed, that proves you need it.

I don’t get to make every objection into evidence that I’m right.

I can ask students to study this history. I can expect them to take it seriously. I don’t get to force them to interview a relative or turn a private family reckoning into schoolwork. That’s the line I’m trying to get right.

But this is the history of the city they live in. It happened in neighborhoods they know, to people some of them still see at family gatherings or in the grocery store. The textbook gives it one paragraph. We can do better than that without requiring anyone to put a grandparent on trial.

And yes, Jess, I could get burned.

I’ve had tenure since 2021. That matters, and I’m not going to act as though I’m risking instant unemployment by disagreeing with my principal. But Halvorsen still controls my schedule. He still has a say in who gets AP. There are plenty of ways for this to make my working life harder without anyone firing me.

I’m scared of that. Not dramatically scared. More the kind where I’m trying to grade something and catch myself rehearsing a conversation that hasn’t happened yet.

I don’t feel especially brave, and I don’t want to write myself into a story where I’m the brave teacher and everyone else is afraid of history. The parent is worried about her kid. You’re worried about your friend. I have responsibilities to both the students doing the assignment and the people they might interview. There’s plenty here for me to reconsider.

I just haven’t heard a good reason to quietly drop the whole thing.

At 3:15 on Thursday, November 19, I’m going to sit down with Halvorsen and the parent. I’m going to listen. I’m going to explain the alternatives and why I should have offered them already. And I’m going to make the case for keeping the project.

You don’t have to agree that it’s worth the trouble. I know your text came from love, not indifference. I’m glad you’re still the person who will tell me when you think I’m being an idiot, even when I respond by writing an entire blog post.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. You can ask how it went, and then, if necessary, whether I’ve eaten anything.
